texts.preamble: Antony P.C vs State Of Kerala on 6 February, 2020
texts.facts: The specific allegation is that the 1st accused, who is the Officer-in-charge of the Resort, sold 2.00 kgs. of Moong Dal, which was kept in the premises, to the Food Safety Officer and the said Moong Dal was found contained a synthetic food colour, namely, Tartrazine, which according to Regulation 3.1.2(6) of the Regulations is not permissible and therefore the article is adulterated.
texts.arguments: The first contention is that Moong Dal is not meant for sale and therefore it was not sold or rather it was seized by the Food Safety Officer. What is sold in a Resort is only articles prepared at the Restaurant and for the preparation of said articles the said additive, namely, Tartrazine, can be used. The Food Safety Officer's contention is that the Moong Dal in its primary form cannot be mixed with an additive, namely, Tartrazine, and therefore it an additive, which is not permissible and it is not a prepared item, which contained Tartrazine. 4. The learned Counsel for the petitioners would contend that only when it is sold can the provisions under the Act is attracted. But Section 38(1)(a)(ii) indicates that the Food Safety Officer may take a sample of any article of food or substance which is found by him on or in any such premises and therefore Moong Dal, which was purchased by him from the 1st accused can be held up for adulteration under the Act, in case it is found to be so. 5. I find that since the Food Safety Officer has the authority to seize and collect samples of food articles kept in the premises, prima facie there is nothing wrong. The next argument raised by the learned Counsel for the petitioners is that petitioners 2 and 3 are the Managing Partner and Partner respectively of the 4th petitioner-Firm and therefore they do not have any direct connection with the alleged sale or seizure of the articles and therefore, they need to be exonerated. The 1st petitioner is a person, who was conducting the business on behalf of the Firm and alleged to be directly responsible. The 2nd petitioner is the Managing Partner of the 4th petitioner-Firm and therefore he also could be held to be responsible for the act of the 1st petitioner.
